title: How Chocolate Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and production of chocolate, from its ancient Mesoamerican roots with the Maya and Aztecs, through the European addition of sugar and the Industrial Revolution innovations of Van Houten, Fry, Lindt and Nestle, to the modern process of growing cacao, fermenting, roasting, grinding, conching and tempering. They also cover cacao varieties, chocolate's health effects and mood impact, theobromine toxicity to dogs, child labor in cacao farming and fair trade, and cultural chocolate traditions. The episode ends with a listener mail from a history teacher about problems in the US education system.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor shout-out
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, shout out Little Bit Sweets' new retail space at Chelsea Market, and preview chocolate as a topic similar to their coffee episode.

segments.title: Ancient chocolate in Mesoamerica
segments.summary: Chocolate consumption dates back to at least the Maya, with residue found in a bowl from around 1000 BC. Early chocolate was a frothy, bitter drink sometimes flavored with cinnamon and chili. The Aztecs adopted it, and it was used as currency and was sacred.

segments.title: Spanish conquest and European sweetening
segments.summary: Spaniards initially disliked the bitter drink, then Europeans added sugar. Cortez brought chocolate to Europe, and demand led to growing cacao in tropical colonies, lowering prices.

segments.title: Industrial innovations in chocolate
segments.summary: Van Houten separated cocoa butter from cocoa powder and developed Dutch cocoa with alkali. Joseph Fry made the first chocolate bar, Lindt developed conching in 1879, and Nestle added milk powder for milk chocolate around 1904.

segments.title: Dark chocolate bitterness and bitter taste
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the bitterness of dark chocolate by percentage and their personal tolerance, linking it to super tasters from an earlier episode.

segments.title: Growing cacao and bean varieties
segments.summary: Cacao trees are trimmed to about ten to twelve feet for harvesting, and pods are picked by hand because they do not ripen together. About two and a half million farmers grow most of the world's cacao, mainly in West Africa, especially Ivory Coast. The three main varieties are Forastero, Criollo, and Trinitario, and terroir affects flavor.

segments.title: Processing cacao: fermenting, roasting, grinding, conching, tempering
segments.summary: Pods are fermented under banana leaves for about a week, beans are graded and sold, then roasted to create flavor through the Maillard reaction. Nibs are cracked and winnowed, ground into chocolate liquor under pressure, separated into cocoa butter and press cake, mixed with sugar and emulsifiers, conched, and tempered to form type five cocoa crystals.

segments.title: Chocolate consumption, health, mood, and dog toxicity
segments.summary: Discussion of chocolate consumption by country (Swiss and Germans eat most, Americans about twelve pounds a year), flavonoids for heart health, a 2007 study showing a short mood boost, and theobromine being toxic to dogs. Child labor on cacao farms and fair trade or organic labels are covered, along with Japan's White Day.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the chocolate discussion and point listeners to howstuffworks.com.
